Q: AI/IDE Integration: Claude Code for VS Code vs. Cursor Models A:

Benefits of each option

Claude Code for VS Code

  • Works inside standard VS Code (no forked editor)

  • More agent-style workflow (plan → apply diff → review)

  • Better suited for larger refactors and structured changes

  • Feels more controlled and deliberate

Cursor (Models)

  • AI-first editor with strong context handling

  • Ability to switch models depending on the task

  • Very efficient for iterative development and exploration

  • More “copilot on steroids” than autonomous agent

When to use which

  • Use Cursor if you:

    • iterate quickly

    • want model flexibility

    • spend a lot of time exploring or reshaping code

  • Use Claude Code for VS Code if you:

    • want a planned, reviewable workflow

    • do larger or riskier refactors

    • prefer staying in stock VS Code

In short:

Cursor optimizes for speed and flexibility.
Claude Code optimizes for structure and control.

Q: RuntimeError: cuDNN error: CUDNN_STATUS_NOT_INITIALIZED using pytorch A:

i faced the same issue on Nvidia Jetson oren nano jetpack v 5.1.x

i uses following method to fix it and it works
check

  1. cat /proc/meminfo | grep -i cma
    If it’s < 512 MB → that’s the problem.
  2. sudo nano /boot/extlinux/extlinux.conf
    Find the line that starts with APPEND (it’s long).
    Add this at the end of that line:

APPEND ............... cma=1024M

Save + reboot

sudo reboot
it works for me

Q: When is it appropriate to use the "Async" suffix when naming a function? Yield, or non-blocking, or both? A:

"When is it appropriate to use the "Async" suffix when naming a function?" - speaking for C#/.NET, only: There is a growing faction of devs that advocate for not using the suffix at all in new code. The reasons being: you can spot "async(ish)" behavior by the async keyword and/or the Task or Task<T> return types (or other awaitable types, but that would be really really unorthodox). Which renders the additional Async suffix only contributing to noise in the code, no signal.

I, personally, am taking no stance on this; just wanted to contribute, that this exists.

Q: What does this package looking icon mean in this UML diagram? A:

Those are visibility indicators. P. 118 (and others) in the UML 2.5 specs:

<visibility> is the visibility of the Operation (see 7.4). <visibility> ::= ‘+’ | ‘-‘ | ‘#’ | ‘~’

P. 246:

The visibility of a packagedElement may be indicated by preceding the name by a visibility symbol (‘+’ for public and ‘-’ for private). Packages may not have protected or package visibility.

and on P 167:

Interestingly there is no place where all symbols are related to their meaning. So you just "guess" it from the order in the diagram that protected is # and package is ~.

The graphical adornments are inventions of the tool creator, so not UML standard. The box icon likely is used for operations and balls for attributes (plus some extra gimmick I can't guess; looks like a key for probably a constant attribute?). The icon top near the name might be derived from a stereotype, but I guess it's just something you find in the tool manual. Not necessarily wrong from a UML perspective, but, as you encountered, simply confusing.

Q: Advice needed: scraping company websites in Python A:

There's no (or little) commonality between web sites. If you're just looking to scrape static data you might do better just to copy and paste manually.

If you want to scrape dynamic data then expect to put significant effort into each separate web site.

Bear in mind that sites with valuable data are implementing increasingly sophisticated defences against automated scraping that might make it impossible to scrape them at all.

In short focus your question if you want some specific advice.
